title: The Team Is Shipping Without A Clear Behaviour Model
excerpt: This situation describes a team shipping features without a shared behaviour model for how the product should act across states, workflows, exceptions, and edge cases. The result is behavioural inconsistency, local decision-making, and interface debt that accumulates during delivery.
metaDescription: A delivery situation where features ship without a shared behaviour model, causing local decisions, product contradiction, and interface debt.
summary: A team is shipping without a clear behaviour model when features and requirements exist, but no governing specification defines how the product should behave as a coherent system. The product can continue to grow while accumulating contradictions across workflows, states, and feature boundaries.
definition: A product is shipping without a clear behaviour model when delivery proceeds without a shared specification of what the product does in each situation, how states relate, and what principles govern decisions not explicitly covered by requirements.
keyFacts: A behaviour model answers how the product should behave, not only what features it contains.
When no behaviour model exists, engineers and designers make local decisions based on local understanding.
Local decisions can produce a product that is internally coherent within individual features but contradictory across the whole product.
Characteristic signals include behavioural contradiction, disproportionate debate for new features, demos that require explanation, and users who cannot form a reliable mental model.
This is classified as a delivery-and-execution situation because the missing artefact is a behaviour specification used during delivery.
The situation is distinct from feature-count incoherence, stakeholder misalignment, and design erosion during development.
Veecle, Hudex, KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and Callsign are used as case evidence for different aspects of behaviour-model absence or specification.
KISPE Space, Raymarine, and Schone Airspace Group describe governing behaviour artefacts, but their artefact counts are not comparable like for like.
bodyMarkdown:
## Shipping without a behaviour model means delivery continues without governing product behaviour

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A product's behaviour model is the answer to how the product should behave. It is not limited to the feature list. It covers what the product does when a user acts, what the product shows in each state, how different parts of the product relate to each other, and what principles govern decisions that the specification does not explicitly cover.

A team is shipping without a clear behaviour model when features, requirements, and backlog items exist, but no coherent model governs product behaviour. Interface decisions are then made locally. Each engineer or designer makes the best decision available for one part of the product, based on a local understanding of what the product should do.

Local decisions accumulate into behavioural inconsistency. The same action can have different outcomes in different parts of the product. The same type of content can be displayed differently depending on where it appears. The product can make sense inside individual features while becoming difficult to explain as a whole.

## This is a delivery-and-execution situation because the missing artefact is a behaviour specification

This situation belongs to delivery and execution because the team is building the product and the missing element is a delivery artefact: a governing behaviour specification. The problem is not that the team is unable to deliver. The problem is that delivery proceeds without the layer that makes the delivered product coherent.

This situation is distinct from too many features without coherence. Feature-count incoherence concerns quantity and product strategy. A missing behaviour model can exist regardless of how many features the product has.

This situation is distinct from stakeholder misalignment. Stakeholder misalignment concerns competing opinions. A missing behaviour model can exist even when everyone agrees on what to ship.

This situation is distinct from design not surviving development. Design erosion concerns a correctly specified design degrading during implementation. A missing behaviour model means there is no governing behavioural specification to survive or fail to survive implementation.

## Behavioural inconsistency is the primary observable signal

The product contradicts itself when the same action has different outcomes in different areas, error states are handled differently per feature, or the same type of data is presented differently depending on where it appears. This is behavioural inconsistency rather than visual inconsistency. A design system can address many visual inconsistencies, but it does not by itself define the governing logic of product behaviour.

New features require disproportionate design debate when no existing model can be used to derive the answer. A decision that should be resolved in a day can take a week because the governing logic has not been established.

Demos require explanation when the product itself does not communicate what it is, what it does, or what the user should do next. In sales demonstrations or investor pitches, team members may need to mediate between the product and the audience.

Users cannot form a reliable mental model when product behaviour is not predictable from the interface. Actions sometimes produce the expected result and sometimes do not. The user cannot infer the whole system's logic because no governing model determined that logic.

## Core vocabulary for this situation

A behaviour model is the governing specification of how a product should behave, including what it does in which situations, how different parts relate to each other, and what principles govern edge cases.

A local design decision is a design decision made without reference to a governing model. In this situation, local design decisions are the unit by which behaviour debt accumulates.

Product incoherence is the aggregate result of many local design decisions made without governing logic. The product behaves in ways that cannot be explained as a whole.

An interface contradiction occurs when different parts of the same product behave according to different local logics that contradict each other.

A behaviour specification is the explicit, shared documentation of what the product should do and how it should behave. In this situation, the behaviour specification is the missing delivery artefact.

Feature velocity without behaviour coherence means features are shipped quickly while interface debt accumulates with every unmoored local decision.

## Veecle and Hudex show products that worked but lacked orientation behaviour

In the Veecle automotive embedded IDE case, the product was already working, actively developed, and had approximately ten beta users at the start of Creative Navy's engagement. Users arriving at the platform could not understand what it was capable of, what the workflow was, or what to do when something went wrong. The AI features felt contextless because no behaviour model had been established for what the AI did, when it operated, or how it related to the rest of the IDE. Loading and processing states were opaque because no behaviour had been specified for what the product should communicate during those states.

The Veecle evidence is client-reported for the outcome. The documented case reports that £2M development funding was unlocked after the redesign that established the behaviour model. The funding was enabled in part because the redesign produced a product that could be demonstrated coherently, so investors could understand what the product was and what it did.

In the Hudex intelligence analysis platform case, the platform had been built and shipped with AI-powered semantic clustering. The missing behaviour model concerned user entry and orientation. The dondogram was the first thing users encountered, without preceding orientation. Users arriving without analyst guidance could not understand what they were looking at, and demos required an analyst to mediate between the product and the audience.

The Hudex evidence is client-reported for the outcome. After the redesign that established the entry behaviour model, 45 existing users rated the product as significantly better, and new users could orient independently.

## KISPE Space documents the governing artefact that this situation lacks

The KISPE Space engagement provides evidence of the artefact that teams lack in this situation: a governing model of what the product does in which states, with principles covering what the specification does not explicitly reach. The engagement concerned a common space operating picture for a UK space systems engineering company.

Creative Navy specified 61 behavioural rules in ten families: geographic and workspace context, time, imagery, satellite services, provenance and uncertainty, notifications, connectivity, briefings, integration and diagnostics, and field presentation. Each rule carried four parts: the trigger, the required response, the guard, and a specific verification check.

Creative Navy also specified six state models and eight cross-module regression checks. These covered area confirmation and query lineage, imagery catalogue and asset retrieval, provider reachability and device observations, local annotation synchronisation, saved live view versus frozen briefing, and notification interaction.

The KISPE Space specification included a change-control rule across artefacts. If a technical fact or an observed behaviour contradicted a direction, its status and reasoning were updated, and every linked journey, behaviour rule, and exception screen was revised in the same change. Modifying the visual prototype while leaving the specification inconsistent was defined as a documentation defect, and a superseded decision received a new record rather than a silent overwrite.

The KISPE Space verification checks and regression checks were specifications of tests. They were explicitly recorded as not executed. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

## Raymarine and Schone Airspace Group show governing behaviour artefacts across hardware and operational systems

The Raymarine engagement applied a governing behaviour artefact to hardware for the next generation of Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF line. A physical input contract covered ten controls, each specified in three conditions: radio view, AIS or menu view, and interrupted state.

The Raymarine physical input contract included five principles. Any context-sensitive button needed a visible label on the active screen. Transmit and receive state needed to remain visible during AIS browsing. A modal event could not silently reinterpret a continuous physical control. Returning from an alert needed to restore a safe and comprehensible task context. Power, volume, transmit, and protected emergency controls were never repurposed as general navigation inputs.

Raymarine acceptance registers ran across the specification set, with close to two hundred observable checks in all. The documented checks included eighteen tests on the physical control contract, twenty-four verification scenarios in the exception catalogue, and ten UI acceptance criteria at handover. Each check was written as an observable condition testable against a prototype, a hardware mockup, or a firmware implementation, not as a subjective preference.

The Raymarine radio was built and released. No fidelity comparison is recorded, so release is not evidence that the built radio matched the delivered design.

The Schone Airspace Group engagement specified 12 principal interaction contracts. Each contract stated the initiating action, the state transition, the visible result, the required source inputs, the exception behaviour, and the conditions by which the design could be checked.

Schone Airspace Group also specified eight operational invariants as the binding acceptance core of the interaction specification: separate inspection from command targeting; separate interface selection from real authority; preserve command transaction semantics; preserve the age of information; preserve warning ownership; preserve context across workspaces; separate live and recorded truth; and no implied command during preparation. The product is built and in test, not deployed.

## Callsign shows policy functionality without a governance behaviour model

Before Creative Navy's engagement, Callsign's fraud detection platform had been built and shipped without a defined behaviour model for how fraud policies should be created, configured, reviewed, and audited. Fraud rules existed across database views and configuration tables with no policy-level object and no specified behaviour for how governance and audit trail aspects of fraud management should work.

Each part of the Callsign system worked, but the aggregate system had no coherent behaviour specification for what a compliance reviewer would encounter and do. The redesign established the policy as the central object, separated configuration and evaluation modes, and treated the audit trail as a workflow output.

The Callsign outcome evidence is client-reported. Bank contracts with Lloyds and HSBC followed demos that demonstrated the behaviour model to risk teams.

## Evidence boundaries for behaviour-model claims

The evidence on this page should not be read as a single comparable metric across engagements. KISPE Space's 61 behavioural rules, Raymarine's acceptance registers, and Schone Airspace Group's 12 interaction contracts count different artefacts for different clients and should not be compared like for like.

KISPE Space verification, acceptance, and regression vocabulary refers to specified checks, not completed testing. Nothing was executed, and no user testing is recorded for those checks. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

Raymarine acceptance registers are specifications. The radio's release is not a fidelity claim, and no commercial or reception figure is recorded. Radio protocol behaviour, channel plans, distress procedure, and final conformity remained Raymarine's responsibility.

Schone Airspace Group contracts and invariants describe the design. The acceptance checks evaluated the design representation, not flight performance. The product is in test, not deployed.

Veecle funding, Hudex user ratings, and Callsign bank contracts are client-reported where stated. They should not be treated as independently measured outcomes.

## Related documentation

This situation is closely related to documentation on product behaviour inconsistency, teams that cannot define good AI behaviour, and products where the model may be good but the product behaviour is not. It is also related to documentation on design not surviving development, too many features without enough coherence, and stakeholders being unable to align on direction, because the distinctions between those situations help define the boundary of this page.

The documented case evidence most directly associated with this situation includes KISPE Space, Raymarine Marine VHF and AIS Radio, Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, and Callsign Fraud Authentication.
